abstract:
Abstract
                  Artificial intelligence-personalized interfaces increasingly use passive behavioral signals generated during ordinary interaction. Such sensing can support personalization but may also heighten perceived surveillance and reduce users’ sense of control. Across two sequential experiments, we tested how data collection type (active sharing vs. passive sensing) and consent design quality (low vs. high transparency/control) shape privacy appraisals, trust, and consent. Study 1 (N = 855) showed that passive sensing increased perceived surveillance and creepiness and reduced trust, consent willingness, and behavioral acceptance, particularly under low transparency/control. High transparency/control increased perceived control and attenuated these effects. Study 2 replicated the principal self-report pattern in a laboratory setting and added eye tracking and galvanic skin response (GSR)/electrodermal activity. Passive sensing increased attention to data-use and decision-relevant elements and produced greater baseline-adjusted electrodermal arousal, with the clearest transparency/control buffering during the decision window. Process measures did not add explanatory value for trust or consent willingness, although an exploratory model indicated that GSR measures improved prediction of behavioral acceptance. Passive sensing should therefore be treated as a consent and privacy design issue, not only as a technical mechanism for personalization.

ur.ai_reason: 实验检验AI个性化界面的知情同意与信任
ur.tldr: 两项实验表明，AI个性化界面的被动感知比主动共享更易引发监控感与不适，并降低信任、同意意愿和行为接受；提升数据使用透明度与用户控制可缓解这些影响。眼动与皮电结果显示，被动感知会增加注意并提高决策期唤醒，透明控制具有缓冲作用。

title: Consent to passive sensing in artificial intelligence-personalized interfaces: perceived surveillance, transparency, and trust
title_zh: 人工智能个性化界面中被动感知的知情同意：监控感知、透明度与信任
